provisions.title: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
provisions.text: The system's authorization functionality does not prevent one user from gaining access to another user's data or record by modifying the key value identifying the data.

provisions.title: Broken Object Level Authorization
provisions.text: Every API endpoint that receives an ID of an object, and performs any action on the object, should implement object-level authorization checks. The checks should validate that the logged-in user has permissions to perform the requested action on the requested object.

examples.label: positive
negative

value.reason: Order PDFs are written to the 'ftp/' directory (routes/order.ts:45). server.ts:294 then serves that same 'ftp' directory publicly at '/ftp' with serveIndex directory listing. The only middleware in front of it is serveIndexMiddleware, and nothing in the Evidence shows it checks who is asking. That differs from the authenticated routes such as '/rest/basket', which use security.isAuthorized(). The checkout that creates these files (POST /rest/basket/:id/checkout, which calls placeOrder) requires a logged-in user. But the files it produces can be listed and downloaded by anyone, so order documents tied to customers (contact data, like the user email held in the User model) sit in a public folder. This matches the positive example: an unauthenticated serveIndex over the same directory that placeOrder writes to, while the negative example puts isAuthorized() in front of the listing. One gap: the Evidence does not show the PDF contents directly, so the email being inside the PDF is inferred from the order flow. Even so, putting per-customer order files in a publicly listed directory with no access control fails the requirement to control access to computer resources that hold personal data.
